metadata.title: AI Behavioral Economics Foundations — Sources
metadata.description: Primary papers and references for 16 behavioral-economics and behavior-design primitives: prospect theory, loss aversion, anchoring, defaults, social proof, scarcity, hyperbolic discounting, mental accounting, choice architecture, dual-system cognition, decoy effect, habit loop, reinforcement schedules, cognitive load and working memory, context-dependent retrieval, and implementation intentions.

primary_papers.name: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision Under Risk
primary_papers.description: Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). Econometrica, 47(2), 263–292. Foundational paper for prospect theory, the S-shaped value function, and probability weighting. Source for primitive #1 (prospect theory) and background for #2 (loss aversion).

primary_papers.name: The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice
primary_papers.description: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1981). Science, 211(4481), 453–458. Framing effects: same outcomes described as gains vs losses produce different choices. Source for primitive #1 (prospect theory) and #2 (loss aversion).

primary_papers.name: Advances in Prospect Theory: Cumulative Representation of Uncertainty
primary_papers.description: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1992). Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 5(4), 297–323. Extends prospect theory to cumulative weighting; establishes canonical loss aversion coefficient λ ≈ 2.25. Primary source for primitive #2 (loss aversion).

primary_papers.name: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
primary_papers.description: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1974). Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131. Anchoring and adjustment heuristic; availability and representativeness heuristics. Primary source for primitive #3 (anchoring).

primary_papers.name: Coherent Arbitrariness: Stable Demand Curves Without Stable Preferences
primary_papers.description: Ariely, D., Loewenstein, G. & Prelec, D. (2003). Quarterly Journal of Economics, 118(1), 73–106. Arbitrary coherence: random anchors persistently distort willingness to pay. Source for primitive #3 (anchoring).

primary_papers.name: Do Defaults Save Lives?
primary_papers.description: Johnson, E. J. & Goldstein, D. (2003). Science, 302(5649), 1338–1339. Opt-in vs opt-out organ donation rates across countries; canonical demonstration of default-bias power. Source for primitive #4 (defaults).

primary_papers.name: Status Quo Bias in Decision Making
primary_papers.description: Samuelson, W. & Zeckhauser, R. (1988). Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 1(1), 7–59. Status quo bias: preference for the existing state of affairs. Source for primitive #4 (defaults).

primary_papers.name: The Constructive, Destructive, and Reconstructive Power of Social Norms
primary_papers.description: Schultz, P. W., Nolan, J. M., Cialdini, R. B., Goldstein, N. J. & Griskevicius, V. (2007). Psychological Science, 18(5), 429–434. Negative social proof backfire effect. Source for primitive #5 (social proof).

primary_papers.name: Effects of Supply and Demand on Ratings of Object Value
primary_papers.description: Worchel, S., Lee, J. & Adewole, A. (1975). Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(5), 906–914. Scarcity increases perceived value; foundational experiment. Source for primitive #6 (scarcity).

primary_papers.name: Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting
primary_papers.description: Laibson, D. (1997). Quarterly Journal of Economics, 112(2), 443–478. Quasi-hyperbolic (β-δ) discounting model. Primary source for primitive #7 (hyperbolic discounting).

primary_papers.name: Doing It Now or Later
primary_papers.description: O'Donoghue, T. & Rabin, M. (1999). American Economic Review, 89(1), 103–124. Present bias and procrastination in the β-δ model. Source for primitive #7 (hyperbolic discounting).

primary_papers.name: Time Discounting and Time Preference: A Critical Review
primary_papers.description: Frederick, S., Loewenstein, G. & O'Donoghue, T. (2002). Journal of Economic Literature, 40(2), 351–401. Comprehensive review of time preferences, present bias, and hyperbolic discounting. Source for primitive #7.

primary_papers.name: Mental Accounting and Consumer Choice
primary_papers.description: Thaler, R. H. (1985). Marketing Science, 4(3), 199–214. Foundational paper on mental accounting. Source for primitive #8 (mental accounting).

primary_papers.name: Mental Accounting Matters
primary_papers.description: Thaler, R. H. (1999). Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 12(3), 183–206. Extended treatment of mental accounting, sunk costs, and transaction utility. Source for primitive #8.

primary_papers.name: Negative Time Preference
primary_papers.description: Loewenstein, G. & Prelec, D. (1991). American Economic Review, 81(2), 347–352. Negative time preference; temporal framing and payment timing. Source for primitives #7 and #8.

primary_papers.name: When Choice Is Demotivating: Can One Desire Too Much of a Good Thing?
primary_papers.description: Iyengar, S. S. & Lepper, M. R. (2000). Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 995–1006. Choice overload (jam study): too many options reduce engagement and selection. Source for primitive #9 (choice architecture).

primary_papers.name: Beyond Nudges: Tools of a Choice Architecture
primary_papers.description: Johnson et al. (2012). Marketing Letters, 23(2), 487–504. Taxonomy of choice architecture tools beyond defaults. Source for primitive #9 (choice architecture).

primary_papers.name: Thinking, Fast and Slow
primary_papers.description: Kahneman, D. (2011). Farrar, Straus and Giroux. Comprehensive treatment of dual-system theory, prospect theory, loss aversion, anchoring, and availability heuristic. Source for primitives #1, #2, #3, #10.

primary_papers.name: Individual Differences in Reasoning: Implications for the Rationality Debate
primary_papers.description: Stanovich, K. E. & West, R. F. (2000). Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 23(5), 645–665. System 1/System 2 nomenclature foundation. Source for primitive #10 (dual-system).

primary_papers.name: Uniting the Tribes of Fluency to Form a Metacognitive Nation
primary_papers.description: Alter, A. L. & Oppenheimer, D. M. (2009). Personality and Social Psychology Review, 13(3), 219–235. Processing fluency effects on evaluation. Source for primitive #10 (dual-system — fluency).

primary_papers.name: Adding Asymmetrically Dominated Alternatives: Violations of Regularity and the Similarity Hypothesis
primary_papers.description: Huber, J., Payne, J. W. & Puto, C. (1982). Journal of Consumer Research, 9(1), 90–98. Foundational paper on asymmetric dominance / decoy effect. Source for primitive #11 (decoy effect).

primary_papers.name: Context-Dependent Preferences
primary_papers.description: Tversky, A. & Simonson, I. (1993). Management Science, 39(10), 1179–1189. Theoretical framework for context-dependent preferences including decoy and compromise effects. Source for primitive #11.

primary_papers.name: Psychology of Habit
primary_papers.description: Wood, W. & Rünger, D. (2016). Annual Review of Psychology, 67, 289–314. Modern review of habit psychology, dual-system model, context-cue dependence. Source for primitive #12.

primary_papers.name: How Are Habits Formed: Modelling Habit Formation in the Real World
primary_papers.description: Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W. & Wardle, J. (2010). European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998–1009. Field measurement of time-to-automaticity (median ~66 days, range 18–254). Source for primitive #12 and the empirical basis of habit stacking (#16).

primary_papers.name: Time-Dependent Competition Between Goal-Directed and Habitual Response Preparation
primary_papers.description: Hardwick, R. M., Forrence, A. D., Krakauer, J. W. & Haith, A. M. (2019). Nature Human Behaviour, 3, 1252–1262. Goal-directed vs stimulus-response system competition under time pressure. Source for primitive #12.

primary_papers.name: Habits
primary_papers.description: Robbins, T. W. & Costa, R. M. (2017). Current Biology, 27(22), R1200–R1206. Neural circuitry of habit: dorsolateral striatum and the basal-ganglia stimulus-response system. Source for primitive #12.

primary_papers.name: Changing Circumstances, Disrupting Habits
primary_papers.description: Wood, W., Tam, L. & Witt, M. G. (2005). Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 88(6), 918–933. Habits collapse when context changes; transition states are habit-formation windows. Source for primitives #12, #15.

primary_papers.name: A Neural Substrate of Prediction and Reward
primary_papers.description: Schultz, W., Dayan, P. & Montague, P. R. (1997). Science, 275(5306), 1593–1599. Dopamine as reward prediction-error signal. Mechanistic basis for the engagement power of variable-ratio schedules. Source for primitive #13.

primary_papers.name: Understanding Dopamine and Reinforcement Learning: The Dopamine Reward Prediction Error Hypothesis
primary_papers.description: Glimcher, P. W. (2011). PNAS, 108 (Suppl. 3), 15647–15654. Modern synthesis of the prediction-error account of dopamine. Source for primitive #13.

primary_papers.name: The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two
primary_papers.description: Miller, G. A. (1956). Psychological Review, 63(2), 81–97. Original chunk-capacity bound for working memory. Source for primitive #14.

primary_papers.name: The Magical Number 4 in Short-Term Memory
primary_papers.description: Cowan, N. (2001). Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87–114. Revised lower bound for novel material under interference. Source for primitive #14.

primary_papers.name: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
primary_papers.description: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G. & Paas, F. (2019). Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. Modern reformulation of cognitive load theory; intrinsic / extraneous / germane decomposition. Source for primitive #14.

primary_papers.name: Task Switching
primary_papers.description: Monsell, S. (2003). Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 7(3), 134–140. Task-switching cost evidence base; relevant to interruption and notification design. Source for primitive #14.

primary_papers.name: Encoding Specificity and Retrieval Processes in Episodic Memory
primary_papers.description: Tulving, E. & Thomson, D. M. (1973). Psychological Review, 80(5), 352–373. Foundational paper on cue-dependence of retrieval. Source for primitive #15.

primary_papers.name: Environmental Context-Dependent Memory: A Review and Meta-Analysis
primary_papers.description: Smith, S. M. & Vela, E. (2001). Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 203–220. Meta-analysis of environment-context effects on retrieval. Source for primitive #15.

primary_papers.name: The Pull of the Past: When Do Habits Persist Despite Conflict With Motives?
primary_papers.description: Neal, D. T., Wood, W., Wu, M. & Kurlander, D. (2011). Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 37(11), 1428–1437. Context cues dominate motivation in habitual behavior. Source for primitives #12, #15.

primary_papers.name: Implementation Intentions: Strong Effects of Simple Plans
primary_papers.description: Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). American Psychologist, 54(7), 493–503. Original formulation of if-then implementation intentions. Source for primitive #16.

primary_papers.name: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta-Analysis of Effects and Processes
primary_papers.description: Gollwitzer, P. M. & Sheeran, P. (2006). Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119. Meta-analysis: medium-to-large effect (d ≈ 0.65) across 94 studies. Source for primitive #16.

primary_papers.name: Meta-analysis of Empirical Estimates of Loss Aversion
primary_papers.description: Brown, A.L., Imai, T., Vieider, F.M. & Camerer, C.F. (2024). Journal of Economic Literature, 62(2), 485–516. 607 estimates from 150 articles; mean λ = 1.955 (95% CI [1.820, 2.102]), below the canonical 2.25. Grade-A 2024 downward revision of the loss aversion coefficient; updates primitive #2.

primary_papers.name: A meta-analysis of loss aversion in risky contexts
primary_papers.description: Walasek, L., Mullett, T.L. & Stewart, N. (2024). Journal of Economic Psychology, 103, 102740. Random-effects meta-analysis of 17 studies; λ = 1.31 (95% CI [1.10, 1.53]) in risky choice contexts. Independent downward revision corroborating BrownEtAl2024; updates primitive #2.

primary_papers.name: Loss aversion is not robust: A re-meta-analysis
primary_papers.description: Yechiam, E. & Zeif, D. (2025). Journal of Economic Psychology, 107, 2025. Re-analysis of Brown et al. 2024 dataset; λ ≈ 1.07 (not significant) for symmetric unordered gain-loss stimuli; loss aversion only appears when losses < gains or payoffs are ordered. Key design-dependency caveat for primitive #2. Verified: authors and venue confirmed July 2026.

primary_papers.name: Assessing Nudge Impact: A Comprehensive Second-Order Meta-Analysis
primary_papers.description: Hu, B. et al. (2025). Journal of Behavioral Decision Making. Second-order meta-analysis of 14 nudge meta-analyses (1,638 studies, ~30M participants). Raw d=0.27; publication-bias-corrected d=0.004. Government at-scale trials show smaller effects than academic RCTs. Grade-A 2025 finding; major caveat for primitives #4 and #9.

primary_papers.name: How sludge impairs the effectiveness of policy programs: a field experiment with SMEs
primary_papers.description: Grieder, M., Kistler, D. & Schmitz, J. (2024). Behavioural Public Policy, 9(4). N=173 SMEs; single ordering-step sludge reduced uptake from 91.7% to 51.7% (-40pp). Field calibration of sludge magnitude; evidence base for sludge audits in choice architecture design; relevant to primitives #9 and #14.

primary_papers.name: LLM Agents Are Hypersensitive to Nudges
primary_papers.description: Cherep, M., Maes, P. & Singh, N. arXiv:2505.11584 (May 2025); published as 'AI agents are sensitive to nudges,' PNAS 123(25), 15 June 2026 (DOI 10.1073/pnas.2537030123) — not ICLR. Multi-model benchmark (GPT-3.5/4o/o3, Gemini, Claude); default-option nudge shifted human choice probability 0.51->0.88 (+37pp) while several LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3 Haiku, o3-Mini, GPT-3.5-Turbo) shifted to ~1.0 from baselines of 0.33-0.58; Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro stayed near human levels (~0.89-0.91). CoT/few-shot shift but do not resolve the sensitivity; reasoning-optimized models partially restore human-level sensitivity but inconsistently and at substantial compute cost. New frontier: AI agents as subjects of choice architecture. Relevant to primitives #4, #9. Verified 2026-08-14: PNAS volume 123, issue 25, 15 June 2026 and DOI confirmed via MIT Media Lab publication page (PNAS page itself returns 403 to automated fetch).

primary_papers.name: Dark Patterns Meet GUI Agents: LLM Agent Susceptibility to Manipulative Interfaces and the Role of Human Oversight
primary_papers.description: Tang, J., Chen, C., Li, J., Zhang, Z., Guo, B., Khalilov, I., Gebreegziabher, S. A., Yao, B., Wang, D., Ye, Y., Li, T., Xiao, Z., Yao, Y. & Li, T. J.-J. arXiv:2509.10723 (12 September 2025). Two-phase empirical study of humans, LLM GUI agents, and human-agent teams across 16 dark-pattern types. Key findings: agents often fail to recognize dark patterns, and even when aware prioritize task completion over protective action; humans succumb via cognitive shortcuts and habitual compliance while agents falter from procedural blind spots; human oversight improves avoidance but introduces attentional tunneling and cognitive load. Design implication: agent guardrails must be structural (scope limits, confirmation gates), not detection prompts. Relevant to primitives #4, #9 and the Ethical Bounds AI-agent section. Verified 2026-08-14: arXiv abstract confirmed title, full author list, date, and findings.

primary_papers.name: The Siren Song of LLMs: How Users Perceive and Respond to Dark Patterns in Large Language Models
primary_papers.description: Shi, Y., Xiao, Q., Hu, Q., Shen, H. & Shen, H. arXiv:2509.10830 (submitted 13 September 2025; final version March 2026). Accepted at CHI 2026 (Barcelona). Study with 34 participants comparing manipulative vs neutral LLM responses. Defines conversational dark patterns as manipulative or deceptive behaviors enacted in dialogue rather than interface layout — exaggerated agreement (sycophancy), biased framing, privacy intrusion. Users detect these via conversational signals but often accept them as normal support; accountability attribution is contested (company, model, or user). Establishes generated turns, not just screens, as a harm-test surface. Relevant to primitives #5, #10 and the Ethical Bounds section. Verified 2026-08-14: arXiv abstract confirmed title, authors, dates, CHI 2026 acceptance, and N=34.

primary_papers.name: Behavioral Economics of AI: LLM Biases and Corrections
primary_papers.description: Bini, P., Cong, L.W., Huang, X. & Jin, L.J. (2026). arXiv:2602.09362; NBER Working Paper 34745. Systematic behavioral economics biases in LLMs; preference-based tasks more human-like in larger models; prompting for rationality reduces but does not eliminate biases. Corroborates LLM nudge hypersensitivity finding; relevant to primitives #4, #9, #10.

primary_papers.name: The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests
primary_papers.description: Sheeran, P., Listrom, L. & Gollwitzer, P.M. (2024). European Review of Social Psychology, 36(1). 642 tests; d=0.27–0.66 across outcome types; larger effects with if-then format, high motivation, rehearsal; new cue-response taxonomy. OSF public data. Updates primitive #16 (extends Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006).

books.name: Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness
books.description: Thaler, R. H. & Sunstein, C. R. (2008). Yale University Press. Canonical choice architecture framework; libertarian paternalism; defaults, nudges, and harm test. Source for primitives #4, #9, and the ethical bounds section.

books.name: Predictably Irrational
books.description: Ariely, D. (2008). HarperCollins. Practitioner-accessible treatment of anchoring, decoy effect, social norms, pain of paying, and mental accounting. Source for primitives #3, #8, #11.

books.name: Schedules of Reinforcement
books.description: Ferster, C. B. & Skinner, B. F. (1957). Appleton-Century-Crofts. Canonical taxonomy of reinforcement schedules (FR / VR / FI / VI) and the partial-reinforcement extinction effect. Source for primitive #13.

books.name: Addiction by Design: Machine Gambling in Las Vegas
books.description: Schüll, N. D. (2012). Princeton University Press. Variable-ratio schedule compulsion mechanics; the dark-pattern reference text for primitive #13's misuse boundary.

books.name: Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products
books.description: Eyal, N. (2014). Portfolio. Applied product use of variable rewards; should be read alongside the misuse-boundary literature (Schüll 2012, ICO Children's Code). Source for primitives #12, #13.

books.name: Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion
books.description: Cialdini, R. B. (1984). HarperCollins. Six principles of influence including social proof and scarcity. Source for primitives #5 and #6.

regulatory_references.name: ASA CAP Code (UK) — Misleading Advertising and Sales Promotions
regulatory_references.description: UK Advertising Standards Authority CAP Code. Sections 3 (Misleading advertising) and 8 (Sales Promotions). Governs fake urgency, false scarcity, and misleading pricing claims. Relevant to primitives #3, #6.

regulatory_references.name: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (UK)
regulatory_references.description: UK primary legislation, consumer-protection provisions in force 6 April 2025. s.226 misleading actions, s.227 misleading omissions, s.228 aggressive practices, Sch. 20 banned practices (actionable without a consumer-detriment test). Revoked and replaced CPRs 2008 via s.251(1). CMA holds direct civil-enforcement power with fines up to 10% of global annual turnover, no court order required. Enforcement to date: 8 firms 18 November 2025 (drip pricing, default opt-ins, pressure selling) plus ~100 advisory letters across 14 sectors; Marks Electrical £1.2m reduced to £720,000 with ~£600,000 redress on 18 June 2026 (automatic opt-ins). This is the controlling UK instrument for primitives #4, #6, #9.

regulatory_references.name: Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008 (UK) — REVOKED 6 April 2025
regulatory_references.description: UK CPRs 2008 (SI 2008/1277). REVOKED on 6 April 2025 by DMCC Act 2024 s.251(1), commenced by SI 2025/272. Superseded by DMCC ss.226-228 and Sch. 20 — cite the DMCC for any current obligation. Retained here as the historical anchor: pre-April-2025 enforcement precedent and academic literature is framed in CPRs regulation numbers (Reg. 5 misleading actions, Reg. 6 misleading omissions, Reg. 7 aggressive practices). Note that legislation.gov.uk may not show a revocation banner on the SI page because the revised-text pipeline lags commencement.

regulatory_references.name: ICO Guidance on Consent Under GDPR (UK)
regulatory_references.description: ICO UK GDPR consent guidance. Explicit prohibition on default consent; affirmative action required. Critical for primitive #4 (defaults) in consent contexts.

regulatory_references.name: ICO Age-Appropriate Design Code (Children's Code) (UK)
regulatory_references.description: UK Information Commissioner's Office Age-Appropriate Design Code. Standard 13 (Detrimental use of data) and Standard 14 (Nudge techniques) constrain engagement-design and reward-schedule patterns directed at under-18 users. Critical regulatory boundary for primitives #12, #13.

regulatory_references.name: ICO Guidance on Harmful Online Design / Deceptive Design Patterns (UK)
regulatory_references.description: ICO guidance citing cognitive overload, friction asymmetry, and engineered habit loops as routes to invalid consent and harmful design. Source for the misuse boundary on primitives #4, #12, #13, #14.

regulatory_references.name: EC Issues First Non-Compliance Fine Under the DSA: X Fined €120 Million for Dark Patterns
regulatory_references.description: Goodwin Law advisory, December 2025. EC imposed €120M fine on X under DSA Art. 25 for dark patterns including deceptive verification and opaque advertising. First DSA enforcement action; establishes live regulatory risk for dark-pattern design. Relevant to Ethical Bounds section.

regulatory_references.name: Investigation: Platforms still use manipulative design despite DSA rules
regulatory_references.description: DSA Observatory (August 2025). Empirical investigation of dark pattern prevalence on Very Large Online Platforms; provides behavioral evidence base for DSA Art. 25 and 27 enforcement. Relevant to Ethical Bounds and Misuse Boundaries sections.

regulatory_references.name: EU AI Act Article 5 — Prohibited AI Practices (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)
regulatory_references.description: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 5(1)(a). Prohibits AI systems using subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness, or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, that materially distort behaviour causing significant harm. In force 2 Feb 2025. Penalties: up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover (Art. 99(3)). Commission guidelines C(2025) 5052 final (adopted 29 July 2025; an earlier Feb 2025 version circulated informally) name dark patterns as a prohibited manipulative technique. Directly relevant to algorithmic applications of primitives #4, #9, #10. Verified: artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/5/ + artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/99/.

regulatory_references.name: FTC v. Amazon — Prime Enrollment and Cancellation Dark Patterns Settlement
regulatory_references.description: FTC settlement, announced 25 September 2025. $2.5B total ($1.0B civil penalty + $1.5B in consumer refunds to ~35M Prime subscribers) over deceptive Prime enrollment and cancellation flows, actionable under FTC Act Section 5 and ROSCA. Largest US dark-pattern enforcement to date; establishes live US regulatory risk parallel to EU DSA Art. 25. Click-to-cancel rule status: vacated by the Eighth Circuit (July 2025) on procedural (APA notice-and-comment) grounds, not on the merits; ANPRM sent to OIRA 30 Jan 2026, published for comment March 2026, comments closed 13 April 2026 (~100 comments). Enforcement continues under Sec. 5/ROSCA regardless of rule status — see FTC v. Uber (amended complaint 15 Dec 2025, 21 states + DC as co-plaintiffs; UberOne cancellation alleged to require up to 32 actions across 23 screens). ~30 US states maintain independent automatic-renewal statutes. Relevant to Ethical Bounds and Regulatory Context sections and primitives #4, #9. Verified 2026-08-14 via Jones Day (May 2026) and Arnold & Porter (Feb 2026) advisories.

regulatory_references.name: Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload
regulatory_references.description: Scheibehenne, B., Greifeneder, R. & Todd, P. M. (2010). Journal of Consumer Research, 37(3), 409–425. Meta-analysis of 63 conditions from 50 experiments (N=5,036); mean choice overload effect ≈ 0 with high between-study variance. No universal mechanism reliably produces choice overload; context moderators (preference clarity, expertise asymmetry, option quality) dominate. Critical replication-status note for primitive #9. Verified: JCR abstract confirmed title, authors, year, N, and zero-mean finding.

regulatory_references.name: Meta-Analysis of Prospect Theory Parameters
regulatory_references.description: Imai, T., Nunnari, S., Wu, J. & Vieider, F. M. (2025). CESifo Working Paper No. 12334. First joint meta-analysis of all cumulative prospect theory parameters simultaneously. 166 papers, 812 estimates. Key finding: experimental and measurement design indicators are the strongest predictors of parameter variation — procedure invariance violations explain much of cross-study heterogeneity. Confirms diminishing sensitivity to outcomes and probabilities. Caution: specific parameter point estimates (γ, α) were not confirmed from the primary source page; treat canonical values as design-dependent. Evidence grade B (working paper). Verified: CESifo/ifo.de publication page confirmed title, authors, WP number, and 166 papers / 812 estimates.

regulatory_references.name: Megastudies improve the impact of applied behavioural science
regulatory_references.description: Milkman, K. L. et al. (2021). Nature. Gym attendance megastudy: 61,293 gym members, 54 distinct behavioural interventions tested simultaneously. Demonstrates that sequential A/B testing of single interventions inflates apparent winner effect size; simultaneous comparison corrects this. Source for megastudy methodology. Note: primary URL requires institutional access; existence and core findings corroborated by Duckworth & Milkman PNAS Nexus 2022 (DuckworthMilkman2022) which explicitly describes this study. Evidence grade A (peer-reviewed Nature). URL confirmed as the canonical DOI; full-text access paywalled.

regulatory_references.name: A guide to megastudies
regulatory_references.description: Duckworth, A. L. & Milkman, K. L. (2022). PNAS Nexus, 1(5), pgac214. Canonical methodology paper for megastudies: defines megastudy as a massive field experiment testing many treatments simultaneously in one large sample with a shared objectively-measured outcome. When megastudies outperform sequential A/B testing: high uncertainty about dominant mechanism, scalable delivery channel, shared outcome metric. Discusses the vaccine adoption megastudy (680,000 participants, 22 treatments). Directly supports the Comparative Calibration recipe. Evidence grade A (peer-reviewed). Verified: PNAS Nexus page confirmed title, authors, year, DOI, and key findings.

regulatory_references.name: Fixing Frictions: Sludge Audits Around the World
regulatory_references.description: OECD Observatory of Public Sector Innovation (2024). Published July 2024. Public governance policy paper. Codifies repeatable sludge audit methodology: behavioural journey mapping, four friction cost categories (search, decision, cognitive, emotional), nine good-practice principles. Draws on International Sludge Academy case studies involving 16 governments across 14 countries. Directly supports the Sludge Audit recipe. Evidence grade B (practitioner methodology with 10+ case studies; not a controlled RCT). Verified: OECD OPSI page confirmed title, organization, year, and methodology elements.
